heading: What is a statechart?
text:
A statechart is a state machine whose states can contain other states.

First, the thing it builds on. A state machine is always in exactly one of a few named states (the rounded boxes). When an event happens, it follows the arrow labelled with that event. The dot marks where it starts.

Try it: press TOGGLE and the lamp moves between its two states.

A statechart adds two things. The next two steps show one each.

heading: A state can be a box of states
text:
A state can be a box of states, a parent, and any event its children (the states inside it) don't handle goes to the parent.

Here the lamp's on is a box holding dim and bright. TAP is drawn on the children. SWITCH is drawn once, on the box. Entering the box lands on the child its dot points to.

Press SWITCH, TAP, then SWITCH again. The trace shows who is asked: the current state first, then its parent, until one has an arrow for that event. If none does, nothing happens.

heading: A state can be split into regions
text:
And a state can be split into regions, each in one state at the same time.

Caps Lock and Num Lock don't depend on each other, so a dashed line splits the keyboard into two regions. It is always in one state on each side: right now caps off and num off.

Every event is offered to every region. The region with a matching arrow moves; the other ignores it.

Careful: side by side doesn't mean two programs running at once. It is one machine, handling one event at a time, that remembers one state per region.

heading: A coffee machine gets a power button
text:
Why that matters: in a plain state machine, behaviour shared by many states must be copied onto each of them.

This coffee machine goes idle → grinding → brewing → ready, and back to idle when you take the cup. Now add a power button: from any of those four, POWER_OFF must lead to off.

heading: Four copies of one arrow
text:
You said 2. Each of the four states needs its own arrow. The answer is 4.

Give a coffee machine a power button, and idle, grinding, brewing and ready each need their own POWER_OFF arrow: four copies of the same idea.

Each copy is a chance to forget one. Add a descaling state next year and someone must remember a fifth.

heading: One arrow on the box
text:
Put the four in a box called on, and one POWER_OFF on the box does the job.

None of the four has its own POWER_OFF arrow, so the event goes up to their parent, which has one. Same behaviour, one arrow instead of four, and any state added to the box later gets power-off for free.

Try it: press POWER_ON, START and GROUND to reach brewing, then POWER_OFF, and follow the trace.

heading: Shared behaviour goes on the parent
text:
This isn't about coffee. Whenever several states react to an event the same way, a plain machine needs one arrow per state; a statechart needs one arrow on their parent.

a checkout where CANCEL works on every step
a phone call where HANG_UP works while ringing, talking or on hold
a game where PAUSE works in every level

Boxes can sit inside boxes. An unhandled event keeps climbing, one parent at a time, until a state handles it or there are no parents left.

heading: A player with two separate features
text:
A music player is playing or paused, and, separately, muted or unmuted. Either can change without touching the other.

A plain state machine is in exactly one state, so each state has to describe both features at once, like “paused and unmuted”. Plain machines are often called flat: no boxes, no regions.

heading: One flat state per combination
text:
You said 4. Right.

Independent features multiply. A player that is playing or paused, and muted or unmuted, needs one flat state per combination, four of them, and each new on/off feature doubles that: 8, 16, 32…

The arrows double too: MUTE is drawn twice, once from each playback state. Try it.

heading: Booleans hide the impossible
text:
A boolean is a true-or-false variable. Programs often track a player with two of them: isPlaying and isPaused.

Booleans hide the same problem: isPlaying and isPaused can both be true, which should be impossible. Two booleans make four combinations, but the player only means two.

heading: Two small machines side by side
text:
Regions keep playback and volume apart, as two small machines side by side, so the impossible combination can't be written.

The playback region is always in exactly one of paused or playing. There is no state for “both”, so it can't happen, and no code has to prevent it.

Send events: MUTE is drawn once, and the playback region simply ignores it.

heading: Regions add; flat states multiply
text:
Each region adds its own few states; a flat machine needs every combination. With k on/off features, regions draw 2 × k states, a flat machine needs 2 × 2 × … (k times).

Drag the slider and watch both drawings grow.

It holds for bigger features too. Add speed (1×, 1.5×, 2×) to the player: flat needs 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 states; regions need 2 + 2 + 3 = 7.

Same shape elsewhere: a car's gear, headlights and wipers; text that is bold, italic and underlined.

heading: Can a statechart do more?
text:
A common belief: statecharts are a more powerful kind of machine, able to describe behaviour a plain state machine can't.

Look at the player statechart. Could some plain state machine behave exactly like it, for every sequence of events?

heading: Same behaviour, smaller drawing
text:
You said yes. That is the misconception. The answer is no.

Nothing new becomes possible: flatten any statechart and you get an ordinary state machine with the same behaviour. To flatten, make one state per combination of region states, and copy each arrow on a box onto every state inside it.

Send the same events to both machines: they always agree.

What you gain is a drawing the size of the idea instead of the size of every combination, so it stays readable as the product grows.

heading: A region inside on
text:
You said a new region inside on. Right.

The frother is independent of the coffee, so it is its own small machine: a region beside the coffee loop, two states, two arrows. POWER_OFF stays one arrow on the box and leaves both regions.

You said 6. Adding two states is what the regions do; flat states multiply. The answer is 8.

The flat machine doubles: every coffee state now comes with froth off and froth on, each needing its own POWER_OFF.

heading: The sentence to remember
text:
A statechart is a state machine that can nest states and run parts side by side, so shared behaviour is written once and independent features don't multiply.

The coffee machine shows both: one POWER_OFF on the on box, and a frother region that adds two states instead of doubling the rest.
